en: Thus have I heard: Majjhima Nikāya 112, the Chabbisodhanasutta (The Discourse on the Sixfold Purification) Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“In this case, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu declares final knowledge:”
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being,’ he says.
Monks, the speech of that monk should neither be welcomed nor rejected.
Without welcoming it and without rejecting it, a question should be asked:
“Friends, these four modes of expression were rightly proclaimed by the Blessed One—the one who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
What are the four?

Speaking of what has been seen as having been seen; speaking of what has been heard as having been heard; speaking of what has been sensed as having been sensed; speaking of what has been cognized as having been cognized.”
“Friends, these four modes of expression have been rightly proclaimed by the Blessed One—who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
How does the Venerable One know, how does he see, so that through these four modes of expression his mind is liberated from the taints by non-clinging?

“Bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is completely liberated through final knowledge, it is in accordance with the Dhamma to declare this:”
“Friend, regarding what is seen, I dwell without means, without recourse, independent, unbound, liberated, and dissociated, with a mind that has transcended all boundaries.
Regarding what is heard, friend...
[as before] ...Regarding what is sensed, friend...”
“Friends, when there is something cognized, I dwell without means, without support, independent, unbound, and liberated, with a mind that is detached and free from boundaries.
It is for one who knows thus and sees thus, friends, that the mind is liberated from the taints through non-clinging regarding these four modes of expression.
Monks, the speech of that monk should be welcomed and rejoiced in as “Excellent!”
Having rejoiced and expressed appreciation for what was said with the word “Excellent,” one should ask a further question:
“Friend, these five aggregates of clinging have been rightly proclaimed by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Which five?”

"Namely: the form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging.
These, friends, are the five aggregates subject to clinging, which have been rightly proclaimed by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
But how does the Venerable One know, and how does he see, so that his mind is liberated from the taints through non-clinging with regard to these five aggregates subject to clinging?"

“Monks, for a monk whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is completely liberated through final knowledge, this is a discourse in accordance with the Dhamma that may be given:
‘Friends, having understood that form is weak, subject to fading away, and not a ground for consolation,

through the destruction, fading away, cessation, relinquishment, and renunciation of those attachments, clingings, mental fixations, adherences, and underlying tendencies toward forms, my mind is liberated.’”
"I understand my mind.
Friend, as for feeling... [as before] ...friend, as for perception..."
"Friends, having understood that volitional formations are weak,

subject to fading away, and not providing consolation— and likewise, friends, having understood that consciousness is weak, subject to fading away, and not providing consolation— I was liberated through the destruction,
fading away, cessation, relinquishment, and renunciation of those approaches, clingings, mental fixations, adherences, and underlying tendencies toward consciousness."
‘I understand my own mind.
It is when one knows thus and sees thus, friends, that the mind is liberated from the taints through non-clinging with respect to these five aggregates subject to clinging.
Monks, the speech of that monk should be welcomed and rejoiced in as “well said.”
Having rejoiced and expressed approval at those words, saying “Excellent!”, one should ask a further question:
“Friend, these six elements have been rightly proclaimed by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Which six?”
“The earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the space element, and the consciousness element— these, friend,
are the six elements that have been rightly proclaimed by the Blessed One, the one who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
But how does the Venerable One know, how does he see, so that through these six elements his mind is liberated from the taints by non-clinging?”

“Bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is completely liberated through final knowledge, this is a statement in accordance with the Dhamma:
‘Friends, I did not approach the earth element as self, nor did I approach a self as dependent on the earth element.’”

"I understand: 'My mind is liberated through the destruction, dispassion, cessation, relinquishment, and letting go of whatever supports for the earth element there are—those acquisitions, mental fixations, adherences, and underlying tendencies.
Likewise, friend, regarding the water element...
and the fire element, friend..."
"Friends, I did not approach the air element as self,
nor did I approach the space element as self, nor did I approach the consciousness element as self, nor did I approach a self dependent on the consciousness element."

‘Whatever clinging to acquisitions, mental fixations, adherences, and underlying tendencies that depend on the consciousness element—through their destruction, fading away, cessation, relinquishment, and abandonment, I understand: “My mind is liberated.
It is when I know thus and see thus, friends, that my mind is liberated from the taints through non-clinging with respect to these six elements.
Monks, the words of that monk should be welcomed and rejoiced in as excellent.
Having rejoiced and expressed appreciation for what was said with the words “Excellent!”, one should ask a further question:
“Furthermore, friend, these six internal and external sense-bases have been rightly proclaimed by that Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Which six?”
"The eye and forms, the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena— these, friends,
are the six internal and external sense bases rightly proclaimed by the Blessed One, the Knower, the Seer, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One. How, venerable sir,
does the Venerable One know, how does he see, so that through non-clinging his mind is liberated from the taints in these six internal and external sense bases?"

“Bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is completely liberated through final knowledge, this is the appropriate discourse for explanation:

‘Friend, whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving, and whatever engagement, clinging, mental standpoints, adherences, and underlying tendencies there are regarding the eye, forms, eye-consciousness, and things cognizable by eye-consciousness— of these...’”
"Through its destruction, fading away, cessation, relinquishment, and renunciation, I understand: 'My mind is liberated.
In the ear, friend, regarding sounds and ear-consciousness...
In the nose, friend, regarding odors and nose-consciousness..."
Friends, whatever desire there is for tastes in the tongue, for tongue-consciousness;
friends, whatever desire there is for tangibles in the body, for body-consciousness;
friends, whatever desire there is for mental phenomena in the mind, for mind-consciousness, and for those phenomena cognizable by mind-consciousness...

"Whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving, whatever underlying tendencies of attachment, grasping, mental fixation, and latent bias—through their destruction, fading away, cessation, relinquishment, and abandonment, I understand: 'My mind is liberated.
It is by knowing thus and seeing thus, friends, that my mind is liberated from the taints through non-clinging regarding these six internal and external sense bases."
“Monks, that monk’s speech should be welcomed and approved with the words, ‘Excellent!
Having welcomed and approved his speech, one should ask a further question:

‘In what way does the Venerable One know, in what way does he see, such that within this conscious body and in all external signs, the underlying tendencies of I-making, mine-making, and the conceit “I am” have been uprooted?’”

“Bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is completely liberated through final knowledge, this is the way that accords with the Dhamma for him to explain:
‘Friends, formerly when I was still a householder, I was ignorant.
Then the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata taught me the Dhamma.’”
Having heard that Dhamma, I acquired faith in the Tathāgata.
Possessed of that acquisition of faith, I reflected thus:
"Household life is cramped, a path of dust; going forth is the open air."
"It is not easy for one living at home to lead the holy life (brahmacariya) in its complete perfection, in its complete purity, polished like a conch shell.
What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on saffron robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness?
Then, friends, after some time, having relinquished a small or a large mass of wealth...

Having abandoned [them], whether it was a small circle of relatives or a large circle of relatives, having shaved off my hair and beard and donned saffron robes, I went forth from the household life into homelessness.
Having thus gone forth, having undertaken the training and the way of life of the bhikkhus, I abandoned the taking of life; from the taking of life...
I abstained from taking life; laying aside the rod and the sword, I dwelt modest, compassionate, and sympathetic toward the welfare of all living beings.
Having abandoned taking what is not given, I abstained from taking what is not given; I took only what was given, expected only what was given, and dwelt with a heart pure and stainless.
Having abandoned unchastity, I lived a life of celibacy, dwelling apart and refraining from sexual intercourse, the common practice of the village.
Having abandoned false speech, I abstained from false speech; I was a speaker of truth, devoted to truth, trustworthy, reliable, and not a deceiver of the world.
Having abandoned malicious speech, I abstained from malicious speech;

having heard something here, I did not repeat it elsewhere for the purpose of dividing these people, nor having heard something there, did I repeat it here for the purpose of dividing those people. Thus, among those who were divided...
I was a reconciler of those who were at variance and one who encouraged harmony; I delighted in concord, rejoiced in concord, and found joy in concord;
I spoke words that create concord.
Abandoning harsh speech, I abstained from harsh speech; I spoke such words as are gentle, pleasing to the ear, affectionate, heart-moving, urbane, agreeable to many people, and dear to many people.
Having abandoned idle chatter, I abstained from idle chatter; I spoke at the proper time, spoke what is true, spoke on the meaningful, spoke on the Dhamma, and spoke on the Vinaya;
I was one who utters speech that is worth treasuring—timely, grounded in facts, measured, and connected with the goal.
I abstained from damaging seeds and plants; I ate only once a day, refraining from eating at night and abstaining from food outside the proper time.
I abstained from dancing, singing, music, and the witnessing of spectacles.
I abstained from wearing garlands, using perfumes and unguents, and from the adornment and beautification by ornaments.
I abstained from high and luxurious beds and seats.
I abstained from accepting gold and silver;
I abstained from accepting raw grain;
I abstained from accepting raw meat.
I abstained from accepting women and girls;
I abstained from accepting male and female slaves;
I abstained from accepting goats and sheep.
I abstained from accepting chickens and pigs;
I abstained from accepting elephants, cattle, horses, and mares;
I abstained from accepting fields and land.
I abstained from the practice of running errands and acting as a messenger;
I abstained from buying and selling;
and I abstained from cheating with false weights, false measures, and false balances.
I abstained from suborning, deceiving, cheating, and crookedness;
I abstained from mutilation, execution, imprisonment, robbery, plunder, and violence.
I was content with robes to protect the body and almsfood to sustain the belly. Wherever I went, I went only after taking these things with me.

"Just as a winged bird, wherever it flies, flies burdened by its own wings, even so, friend, I was content with robes that served for the body and almsfood that served for the belly. Wherever I went, I went taking only these with me.
Endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, I experienced within myself the happiness of blamelessness."
Thus, having seen a form with the eye, I did not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
Since, if one were to dwell with this faculty of the eye unrestrained, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might flow in, I practiced for its restraint;
I guarded the faculty of the eye and attained restraint over the faculty of the eye.
Having heard a sound with the ear … having smelled an odor with the nose … having tasted a flavor with the tongue … [and so forth] …
Having touched a tangible object with the body...
[and so on] ...having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, I did not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
Had I dwelt with this faculty of mind unrestrained, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—would have arisen.
“Mental phenomena might flow into me; therefore, I practiced for their restraint. I guarded the mind-faculty and attained restraint over the mind-faculty.
Possessed of this noble restraint of the faculties, I experienced an unadulterated happiness within.
I acted with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; I acted with clear comprehension when looking ahead and looking aside.”
I acted with clear comprehension when bending and extending my limbs; I acted with clear comprehension in carrying my outer robe, bowl, and inner robe;
I acted with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; I acted with clear comprehension in attending to the calls of nature;
I acted with clear comprehension when walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent.
Thus, endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, endowed with this noble contentment,
endowed with this noble restraint of the sense faculties, and endowed with this noble mindfulness and clear comprehension,
I frequented secluded lodgings: the forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, or a heap of straw.
Then, having returned from my alms round after the meal, I sat down, folding my legs crosswise, setting my body erect, and establishing mindfulness before me.
Abandoning covetousness for the world, I dwelt with a mind free from covetousness; I purified my mind of covetousness.
Abandoning ill will and hatred, I dwelt with a mind free from ill will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings; I purified my mind of ill will and hatred.
Abandoning sloth and torpor, I dwelt free from sloth and torpor, perceiving light, mindful and clearly comprehending; I purified my mind of sloth and torpor.
Abandoning restlessness and remorse, I dwelt without agitation, with a mind inwardly tranquil; I purified my mind of restlessness and remorse.
Abandoning doubt, I dwelt having crossed over doubt, free from uncertainty regarding wholesome phenomena; I purified my mind of doubt.

Thus, having abandoned these five hindrances—defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—I, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, entered and dwelt in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and filled with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.

With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, I entered and dwelt in the second jhāna, which has internal tranquility and singleness of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and is filled with the rapture and happiness born of concentration. …pe…
I entered and dwelt in the third jhāna… and the fourth jhāna.

With my mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it toward the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.
Thus I directly knew, as it really is: "This is suffering"; I directly knew, as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering"; I directly knew, as it really is:
"This is the cessation of suffering"; I directly knew, as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."
"I understood as it really is: 'These are the taints'; I understood as it really is: 'This is the origin of the taints'; I understood as it really is:
'This is the cessation of the taints'; I understood as it really is: 'This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.
As I knew thus and saw thus, my mind was liberated from the taint of sensual desire, my mind was liberated from the taint of existence, and my mind was liberated from the taint of ignorance."
“When I was liberated, the knowledge arose: ‘It is liberated.
I directly knew: ‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.

It is by knowing thus and seeing thus, friends, that within this conscious body and regarding all external signs, my underlying tendencies toward I-making, mine-making, and the conceit ‘I am’ have been uprooted.”
Monks, that monk’s speech, saying “Excellent!”, should be welcomed and rejoiced in.
Having welcomed and rejoiced in his speech saying “Excellent!”, he should be addressed thus:
“It is a gain for us, friend; it is a great fortune for us, friend.”
“Such a venerable one as you, we regard as a fellow-celibate practitioner.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Elated, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Chabbisodhanasutta, the second, is finished.
